text.content: In the harsh realities of the Mandalorian Wars, your equipment is often as vital as your skills. This chapter details currency and the common, non-combat gear available to characters — medical supplies, survival equipment, tools, and utility items. Weapons, armor, and cybernetics are detailed in the chapters that follow. The availability of specific items may vary greatly depending on location – a core world metropolis will have different markets than a frontier outpost or a war-torn planet.

The standard unit of currency throughout the galaxy is the Galactic Credit Standard (Credits, or “CR.”). Credits are issued by the Galactic Republic and are widely accepted, though black market operations and remote systems may prefer bartering or alternative currencies such as currency made of Aurodium. Credits are often kept on electronic credit chips, transferable to each other via datapads, or terminal interfaces (Requires Computer Operation skill check).

However, stamped Credits made of Aurodium also exist in different denominations, and are semi-common in trading, more so the closer to the outer rim you get. May not be the predominant currency in some locations, and will be mostly worth their weight in Aurodium. In many worlds as you get closer to the core, you may exchange digital credits contained on credit chips for an equal physical physical amount (or vice versa) at banks, merchants, government buildings, corporate offices, or through personal trades. Sometimes with a varying “service fee” percentage of the total transfer attached to the transaction, depending on location.

Combat Stimulants

System Tolerance Rule: A character may safely have one Stimulant active at a time.

  • Taking a second active Stimulant of any type requires an immediate HT-2 roll.
  • On a failure, the character takes 1d toxic damage and is Nauseated (-2 to all attributes and skills) for the duration of the stims due to chemical toxicity. A third stim requires an HT-4 roll, and so on.
  • All Combat Stimulants require a 1-second Ready maneuver to inject and take effect instantly.

Crafting General Gear

Crafting Phases: Building anything in this book takes it through one or more Crafting Phases -- see Construction Markup under Base Materials, later in this chapter, for what a phase is and how each one prices the work. Every item in this chapter takes Phase 1, fabrication, and the skill for that depends on what you are making; the categories below name them, and each item's own Construction Skill column names the one it uses. An item carrying electronics also takes Phase 2, Software Initialization, which is Computer Programming at IQ/Hard. Nothing here takes a third.

  • Medical & Pharmaceuticals (Stims, Medpacs, Antidotes): Pharmacy (Synthetic) to synthesize and mix the raw compounds, or Chemistry at a default penalty to skill.
  • Communication, Data & Electronics (Commlinks, Slicer Gear, Sensors): Electronics Repair (Comms, Computers, or Security) or Engineer (Electronics) for assembly and circuitry routing.
  • Tools, Restraints & Survival Gear (Binders, Hydrospanners, Water Purifiers): Machinist, Mechanic or Armoury depending on the physical item. A shelter is fabric rather than hardware -- see Fabric Goods, below.
  • Explosives (Detonite Charges): Demolitions or Chemistry to safely mix and stabilize the detonite compound.
  • Fabric Goods (Shelters, Tarpaulins): Sewing to cut and stitch the panels and seal the seams.
  • Rations & Preserved Food: Cooking to prepare, portion and seal food that will keep in the field. Fresh food otherwise spoils in a couple of days unless preserved (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.QD9SOsp2PLsi7llq]{Chapter 1}: Eating Well).
  • Cordage (Synth-rope, Line): Knot-Tying to lay and finish the strands into working line.
  • Power & Energy Components (Power Cells, Vibration Generators): Electronics Repair (Power Systems) to build and charge the cell or tune the generator.
  • Software Initialization (Cross-Category Requirement): Any item with an integrated computer, operating system, or complex electronic interface (e.g., Slicer Gear, high-end Sensors, Commlinks, Electronic Binders, and Data Pads) requires a successful Computer Programming roll to function. This is rolled after the physical assembly is complete.

Base Time:

  • Hardware & Electronics: 1 hour of continuous labor per pound of the final scaled weight.
  • Pharmaceuticals & Consumables: 1 hour of continuous processing/mixing per dose or single-use item (e.g., one computer spike or one stimpack).
  • Software Initialization: 1 hour of coding and system configuration for complex items requiring a Computer Programming roll.
  • Crafting in Quantity: A single run may produce any number of identical items. Materials and time both multiply by the count -- ten doses cost ten doses’ materials and ten times the clock. The rolls do not: one roll per phase, however many units are in the run, at whatever workspace, Blueprint and Extra Time modifiers apply. A failure therefore applies its loss to the run’s whole materials, which is what spoiling a batch means. Large runs are a gamble by construction -- one roll decides all of it.

Workspace Modifiers:

  • The Four Tiers: Every crafting chapter uses the same four-step workspace scale -- improvised tools at -5, a basic toolkit at -2, a proper dedicated workspace at +0, and a top-tier facility at +2. Each chapter names the top two for its own trade, so a Dedicated Workshop, a Dedicated Cyber-Clinic and a Dedicated Tech-Bay are all the +0 tier, and an Advanced Research Facility, a High-End Facility and an Advanced Droid Foundry are all the +2. The names change with the work; the numbers never do.
  • Improvised/Field Tools (-5 to skill): Using pocket multi-tools, a campfire, or crude field-splicers.
  • Basic Toolkit (-2 to skill): Using portable electronics repair kits, basic field medkits, or a standard mechanic’s satchel.
  • Dedicated Workshop/Lab (+0 to skill): A facility specifically outfitted with a commercial chemistry set, electronics soldering bench, or dedicated machining tools.
  • Advanced Research Facility (+2 to skill): Top-tier corporate R&D labs, state-of-the-art medical synthesis bays, or military-grade engineering foundries.
  • Kits, and Working Without One: A named kit -- a Tool Kit, an Electronics Tool Kit, Slicer Gear -- is the portable form of a tier, not a component that must be assembled from parts. It is a single crafted item like any other, and what it buys is a place on the scale above: the kit that removes the improvised penalty is the Basic Toolkit tier in your hands.
  • Working Without One: A character who lacks the kit a task calls for works at Improvised/Field Tools (-5) and still rolls; they are never barred for want of it, however well or poorly equipped they are otherwise.
  • Genuinely Required Items: Where a procedure instead names an item outright -- the blank Datacard a Blueprint or a program is written on, the Datapad or workstation that reads it, the empty hand an injector needs -- that item is genuinely required, and no penalty stands in for its absence.

Taking Extra Time: You may work slower to work better, whatever your tools: double the base time for +1 to the roll, four times for +2, eight times for +3, fifteen times for +4, and thirty times for +5. That is the ceiling. This applies to every crafting, deconstruction and salvage roll in this book, and a crafter at a well-equipped bench benefits from patience exactly as much as one working in the dirt -- the bonus is for the care taken, not for the poverty of the tools.

Failure Conditions:

  • Hardware/Electronics (Physical): A failed assembly skill roll ruins the delicate circuitry or precision housing; 50% of the raw materials are wasted and must be replaced before another attempt can be made.
  • Software (Computer Programming): A failed Computer Programming roll means the physical item is intact, but the device is “bricked” or trapped in a boot loop.
  • No materials are wasted, but the crafter must spend another hour debugging and attempt a new roll before the item can be used.
  • Chemical/Pharma (Synthesis): A failed Pharmacy or Chemistry roll spoils the batch -- the compound is inert, contaminated, or will not bind. All the raw materials for that batch are lost, and the workspace must be cleaned of residue before another attempt. A critical failure breaches containment: make a HT roll or suffer 1d-3 toxic damage and -1 to DX for one hour, as with a failed salvage.

Failure & Critical Failure — the loss fraction: A failed build wastes a flat fraction of its raw materials, 50% on a Failure and 100% on a Critical Failure, and that fraction is what you lose however a result describes the damage -- where a critical failure names the parts it destroys (a detonator's Diatium and Silicon, say), the naming is flavour and the fraction governs. Two cases sit outside it:

  • a spoiled chemical or pharmaceutical batch is lost whole even on a Failure (above);
  • a result that ruins a single finished component and calls for it to be reforged -- rather than wasting raw stock -- destroys one component chosen at random from those worked in that phase, the rest surviving.

Salvaging and Deconstruction, Everywhere: These two work the same way in every crafting chapter, so learn them once.

Salvaging is the fast, generic teardown. Everything blends into one raw-material yield and you get 50% of the weight back, or 75% on a critical success, which may also leave one component intact.

Deconstruction is the careful alternative. About twice as long, and it pays twice over: any finished part comes out whole at its listed price rather than being reduced to material at all, and whatever does get reduced comes back separated by material type at 75%, or 90% on a critical success.

That is the trade. Speed and a blended lump, or time and both your parts and a better return on the rest.

One More Payoff: Deconstruction is also the only teardown that can yield a Blueprint of the item (see Blueprints, below). Salvaging blends the evidence; Deconstruction is the act of learning the construction.

Time per pound scales with delicacy, not weight. 10 minutes for clothing, 15 for weapons and armor, 20 for general gear with electronics in it, 30 for droid parts, and a flat 2 hours for an implant, where the pathways are microscopic and the weight is beside the point. Each chapter states its own figure; they differ because the work differs.

Deconstructing General Gear

For an item built from more than one distinct material -- a Credit Chip’s Data-Crystal, Silicon, and Plastoid, say -- Deconstruction is the careful alternative to Salvaging’s generic melt-down. Instead of one blended raw-material yield, each material comes out separately and at a better rate. A single-material item gains nothing from Deconstructing that Salvaging doesn’t already cover; just Salvage those.

Skills Required: The same skill Salvaging would use for that item’s category (Electronics Repair, Machinist/Mechanic/Armoury, Pharmacy/Chemistry, or Computer Programming for a software-bearing layer).

Base Time: 40 minutes per pound of item weight -- twice Salvaging's 20, in exchange for material-by-material precision.

Success: Recover 75% of each distinct material's raw weight, separately, rather than one blended 50%, and any finished sub-component built into the item -- a Power Cell, a blank Datacard -- comes out whole at its listed price instead of being reduced to material at all.

Critical Success: 90% of each material, separately, and every sub-component survives whole.

Failure / Critical Failure: The same consequences as Salvaging, below -- the attempt is still a delicate teardown, just aimed at precision instead of speed.

Salvaging General Gear

When you reclaim components from general gear—ranging from discarded commlinks and sensor arrays to spent medpacs and industrial binders—you can recover raw materials and functional sub-components.

Skills Required:

  • Electronics & Comms: Electronics Repair (Comms, Computers, or Security).
  • Mechanical & Industrial: Machinist, Mechanic, or Armoury.
  • Chemical & Pharma: Pharmacy (Synthetic) or Chemistry.
  • Software Extraction: Computer Programming (required for any device containing an OS or encrypted data).

Base Time:

  • Hardware & Industrial: 20 minutes of labor per pound of item weight.
  • Pharmaceuticals/Consumables: 15 minutes of labor per dose/unit to safely extract or stabilize raw components.
  • Software/Data Recovery: 30 minutes of deep-system probing to dump memory or extract functional logic boards.

Yield Rates:

  • Standard Success: The character recovers 50% of the raw material weight (metal, plastics, reagents).
  • Critical Success: The character recovers 75% of the raw material weight.

Failure Conditions:

  • Hardware/Mechanical Failure: A failed roll results in the item being warped or shorted. The raw materials are reduced to "Scrap" (10% of their base weight recovered). No useful components are recovered.
  • Chemical/Pharma Failure: A failed roll triggers a containment breach. You must make a HT check or suffer the effects of a mild irritant (1d-3 toxic damage and -1 to DX for 1 hour). All materials are lost.
  • Software/Logic Failure: A failed Computer Programming roll results in a “Data Wipe.” The hardware remains intact, but the proprietary OS, encryption keys, or stored data are permanently deleted.
  • Critical Failure: A catastrophic error occurs. An electrical surge or chemical spill causes 1d-3 damage to the salvager. All materials are destroyed, and the workspace suffers minor damage that requires repair before it can be used again.

Workspace Modifiers:

  • Improvised/Field Tools (-5 to skill): Working in the dirt or on a ship’s deck plating.
  • Basic Toolkit (-2 to skill): Standard portable kits.
  • Dedicated Workshop/Lab (+0 to skill): A clean, static-free, and well-lit environment.
  • Advanced Research Facility (+2 to skill): High-end laboratory or industrial bay with automated sorting/recovery equipment.

Taking Extra Time: To avoid critical failures or ensure high-quality yields, you may spend extra time on a salvage or deconstruction roll exactly as on a crafting roll -- see Taking Extra Time under Crafting General Gear, above.

Construction Markup

Construction Markup: Making something takes it through one or more Crafting Phases -- a phase being one step of the build that needs its own skill roll on the item, like forging a component, assembling the parts, or flashing firmware onto a finished chassis. Every chapter that lets you build something lists its phases in an Assembly Sequence and names the skill each one needs. Each phase adds value, so work through them in order and multiply the item's base by each in turn.

The Base: The base is the sum of what went in: raw materials at their listed Cost/lb, any already-finished item at its own market price, and 20 CR per Character Point of any trait the thing grants (see Traits Have a Price, below).

Work on a Person: Work done on a person rather than on the item -- surgically installing a cybernetic, say -- is not a phase and does not mark anything up; that is a fee the patient pays, not value the object carries.

Markup Tiers: Each phase is multiplied by the tier of the skill that phase actually needs:

  • ×1.5 for an Easy skill (Sewing, Cooking, Knot-Tying)
  • ×2 for Average (Electronics Repair, Mechanic, Machinist, Armoury, Smith, Electronics Operation)
  • ×3 for Hard (Armstech, Lightsaber Construction, Computer Programming, Pharmacy, Chemistry, Engineer)
  • ×4 for Very Hard.

Rounding: Round the final figure up to the next whole credit -- 172.35 becomes 173, 779.25 becomes 780. Round once, at the end: the intermediate products between phases are carried in full, and only the finished price is rounded. Note that this is money, and differs from the game statistics a component grants: Damage Resistance rounds to the nearest whole number with halves going up (see @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.sM4JaeipflPpOZgw]{Chapter 13}), because a merchant rounds a price up and a hit is either stopped or it is not.

Choice of Skill: Where a chapter offers a choice of skill for one phase -- “Computer Programming or Electronics Operation,” say -- the tier follows whichever the crafter actually used, so the cheaper route is the lower tier and the item's listed price assumes the harder skill unless the entry says otherwise.

Optional Phases: A phase that only applies in some cases (a software calibration only an electronic item needs) is skipped entirely by items that do not need it, and those items are cheaper for it.

Who Rolls Does Not Change the Tier: A phase's markup follows the skill the phase needs, and that stays fixed however the roll actually gets made. Three cases come up across this book and only one of them moves the number.

  • A genuine fork is a chapter naming two skills as equally valid for the phase at no penalty -- “Armoury (Cybernetics) or Mechanic (Cybernetics)” -- and there either skill is one the phase needs, so the tier follows whichever was used.
  • A substitute at a penalty is a different skill the chapter allows at a stated cost, like a salvager attempting Armoury (Melee Weapons) at -3 where Lightsaber Construction is required; the phase still needs the original skill and the substitute is simply doing it badly, so the tier does not move.
  • A default is the same skill attempted by someone with no points in it, at @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3}'s default -- nothing about the phase has changed at all.

Only the fork reprices. A lightsaber built by someone defaulting Lightsaber Construction is still marked up at that skill's ×3: the hilt is no cheaper for having been made by an amateur, it is only likelier to have gone wrong.

Imported Parts: A fourth case is not a skill question at all: a method that skips the work by importing a finished part, like @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.o2ZbGiux36xwNCw0]{Chapter 14}'s Method B, which installs firmware salvaged from a datacard instead of coding it.

  • The phase still happened -- someone else did it, and its markup is already inside the price of the part you bought or salvaged (see Already-Finished Components, below). So the item's price does not move either.
  • What moved is your cost, because you had to get hold of the card.
  • An implant whose firmware was installed from salvage is worth exactly what one coded from scratch is worth; the object does not know how it was made.

Already-Finished Components: A part that is itself a finished, purchasable item enters a build at its market price, not at the cost of the materials it was made from.

  • Its market price already contains the markup its own construction earned, and that is true whether you bought it or made it yourself -- making it was a construction phase, and phases add value (see Building From Scratch vs. Buying Parts, below).
  • So a Power Cell contributes 210 CR to whatever it is fitted into, not the 35 CR of Diatium, Silicon and Durasteel it was built from.
  • Do not re-derive a finished part from its materials when it appears in another item's recipe: its price is already settled in the section where it is crafted, and that is the figure to use.

Traits Have a Price: Some components do more than take up space -- they grant the user a real trait, and that is part of what you are buying. Such a component adds 20 CR to its base cost for every Character Point of the trait it grants, alongside its materials, and the whole base is then marked up by the construction skill like anything else.

A worked example. A droid's Motion Sensor is 38 CR of materials plus 10 CP of Detect at 20 CR each, so a base of 238, marked up through its two phases -- Mechanic (Droids) and Electronics Repair (Droids), both IQ/Average, so ×2 each -- to 952 CR.

Pricing a trait the tables don't cost. Read it off @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.fZowiGenjFSpf9el]{Chapter 2}'s attribute costs or @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.o2ZbGiux36xwNCw0]{Chapter 14}'s Common Advantages. A +1 to one named skill or a narrow group of them runs about 5 CP, matching Telescopic Vision. A bonus to an attribute's rolls without the attribute itself is worth about half that attribute's rate, so +1 to HT rolls is 5 CP where +1 HT is 10. Halve again for a real limitation, like a charge that runs out or hardware the item must be linked to.

No trait, no addition. A component that grants nothing prices on materials alone.

A negative trait still costs to build. Use the size of the Character Point figure, not its sign. A droid's Basic Labor processor is IQ 8, Automaton and Reprogrammable -- a net -65 CP, because those traits are limitations on the droid -- but building the thing is 65 CP worth of work either way, so it adds 1,300 CR to the base. The buyer is paying for complexity, not for benefit.

Not the same as trading points for cash. None of this is the 700 CR a player may trade a Character Point for at character creation (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.fZowiGenjFSpf9el]{Chapter 2}): that is a character converting points into money, while this is hardware costing more because it does more.

What the Markup Actually Is: The markup is the value your work adds, and it belongs to whoever did the work. An item is worth the same whether it was bought finished, assembled from bought parts, or built end to end from raw stock -- the object does not know how it was made. What changes is what it cost you. A Commlink is worth 1,398 CR:

  • Buy it finished and you pay 1,398.
  • Buy a Power Cell for 210, mill the rest yourself and assemble, and you spent 233 for something worth 1,398.
  • Buy nothing but raw material, build the cell and then the commlink, and you spent 58.
  • The 1,340 CR you did not spend is not a discount. It is the markup you would have paid someone else, kept because you did the work, and it is exactly your profit if you sell.
  • This is why a purchased part enters at its market price rather than at the cost of its ingredients: the person who made that part already earned their markup, and you are paying it. If you would rather not, make the part yourself.

Building From Scratch vs. Buying Parts: A crafter who builds every component themselves, starting from raw materials, goes through every phase along the way and pays each one's markup. Buying pre-made components instead skips the earlier material-to-part phases, since someone else already worked them -- but the assembly phase still applies whenever those parts are put together into a finished item.

Blueprints

A Blueprint is a complete construction schematic for a single item, recorded on a Datacard. A “single item” means a single build, material and all: the same design in a different material is a different item with its own Blueprint -- a Face Plate in Plasteel and the same plate in Durasteel are two schematics, and each catalogue row that names a material (Face Plate (Plasteel), Combat Suit (Durasteel)) is one such item with its own plan. A plan builds only the material it records; a material pairing no catalogue row offers is an original design (the Design Phase, below). The card is physically identical to any blank Datacard (0.28 lbs, 174 CR); only the content differs.

Card as Medium: A Datacard is always a medium, never the thing you are paying for: its 174 CR buys the medium, and anything above that is the content written on it -- a Blueprint's design value here, a Programming Fee for the firmware of a belt (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.sM4JaeipflPpOZgw]{Chapter 13}), an implant (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.o2ZbGiux36xwNCw0]{Chapter 14}) or a droid Processor (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.1ZEtj9W2Z8w75PYC]{Chapter 17}).

Keeping the Card: The card is kept only when the content has to stay readable on it, which is why a Blueprint keeps its card and a firmware flash does not: flashing copies the program into the device's own circuit, and the card reverts to blank and is reused. So a Blueprint is a thing you own, carry and can sell, while a Datacard used to flash firmware is a tool the crafter supplies and takes home again. These are two different cards.

  • A firmware-bearing build -- a belt, shield or face gadget (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.sM4JaeipflPpOZgw]{Chapter 13}), an implant or prosthetic (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.o2ZbGiux36xwNCw0]{Chapter 14}), or a droid Processor or Memory Core (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.1ZEtj9W2Z8w75PYC]{Chapter 17}) -- needs both in hand: the Blueprint that says how to assemble the hardware, and a firmware Datacard carrying the program that runs on it. The Blueprint alone will not build the item.
  • The firmware card you either write yourself (its Programming Fee and a Computer Programming roll) or hold already loaded (a catalogued Datacard, or firmware salvaged from a like item); flashing it into the finished hardware is a Crafting Phase of the build.
  • Firmware burned in at the factory -- droid sensors and reflex wiring -- is the exception, using no swappable card.

Durability: A Blueprint does not wear out: any number of items can be built from it.

Every Build Has an Origin: The crafter must be able to name where the plan came from, and there are exactly three answers. Catalog: the item appears in this book’s tables, so its Blueprint is public -- cheap to buy from any vendor who sells the item (see Buying a Blueprint, below), or recorded from a Deconstruction. Reverse-Engineered: a Blueprint written during a successful Deconstruction of the item. Original Design: a Blueprint the character authored through the Design Phase, below. Building anything -- catalog or custom -- requires the Blueprint in hand: owning an item, or knowing it exists, is not knowing how to make one, which you learn only by taking one apart or buying the plan. What a catalog item’s public Blueprint grants is easy, lawful, inexpensive access to the plan, never a way to build without one. Original designs are the one thing no shop sells.

Reading and Writing: Writing a Blueprint, copying one, or reading one at the start of a build requires at minimum a Datapad or a proper workstation, plus a successful Computer Operation roll. A bare Datapad counts as a Basic Toolkit (-2) on the Four Tiers; a workstation is a Dedicated Workshop (+0) or better. Without at least a Datapad the operation is simply impossible.

Blank Card Required: Writing also needs a blank Datacard to write to, in hand before the roll -- whether the Blueprint is being recorded from a Deconstruction, authored through the Design Phase, or copied from another card. A schematic has nowhere to go without one, and no workspace tier, Blueprint bonus or Extra Time stands in for its absence (see Kits, and Working Without One). Reading needs only the written card itself.

The Write Roll: Unless an entry below states its own, a write is one hour's work and a Computer Operation roll; Failure leaves the card undamaged and the write can be re-attempted after another hour; Critical Failure bricks the card pending a Computer Programming roll at -2 to unlock it. Extra Time applies to a write as to any other roll (Taking Extra Time, above), and so does the workspace tier. That is the roll every entry below means by “the write roll”; a reading is the same roll against the written card, with the same outcomes.

Writing One from a Deconstruction: Requires a successful Deconstruction -- never a Salvage, which blends the item into scrap and teaches nothing about how it went together -- plus a blank Datacard in inventory and the Computer Operation roll above, made during the teardown. Failure: the write doesn't take; the card is undamaged and can be re-attempted after another hour. Critical Failure: the card is bricked pending a Computer Programming roll at -2 to unlock it. The finished Blueprint is Generation 0 and proven -- the item existed and worked.

Building from a Blueprint: Declare the Blueprint at the start of the build and make the read roll -- every build, catalog or custom.

  • Failure: the schematic will not resolve; the card is undamaged, and the read can be re-attempted after another hour.
  • Critical Failure: the card is bricked pending a Computer Programming roll at -2 to unlock it, just as with a failed write.
  • A proven Generation 0 Blueprint is the baseline the tables assume -- no modifier to the build’s Crafting Phase rolls; each generation of the card removed imposes a cumulative -1 (see Copying and Generations, below).
  • An unproven design instead imposes -1 until its first successful build proves it.
  • A lightsaber Blueprint covers the hardware phases only -- Crystal Attunement is personal, and can never be recorded.
  • Lightsaber assembly is itself the exception to the rule that every build needs a Blueprint: a character with Lightsaber Construction (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3}) is trained to build lightsabers and assembles one from its parts with no Blueprint at all. The training covers assembly only -- the component parts (handgrip components and internal modules), when the character manufactures them rather than buying them, are ordinary builds that need their own Blueprints like anything else.

The Design Phase (Original Designs): Before any material is cut, the designer drafts the schematic. This is a Phase 0 preceding the chapter's normal Crafting Phases, and it follows the shape @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.o2ZbGiux36xwNCw0]{Chapter 14} already uses for prosthetic blueprinting.

  • The Roll: Engineer with a specialty matching the item -- Weapons Systems for weapons, Armor for armor and clothing systems, Cybernetics for implants, Droids for droid parts. A crafter without Engineer may attempt it with the item's own crafting skill at -4.
  • The Vocabulary: A design combines only what the tables already contain -- existing slots, components, materials, and priced capabilities -- and its cost, weight, and stats derive from its parts exactly as any catalog item's do. Adding to the tables themselves (a new material, a capability no trait prices, a change to the slot model) is the GM's decision, not a skill roll. A capability delivered by firmware -- a belt or implant that grants a trait, a droid Processor that raises a stat -- is one of these priced capabilities: it enters the design at its Programming Fee (20 CR per CP), and the finished item still builds only with its firmware Datacard in hand alongside the Blueprint (Keeping the Card, above), exactly as a catalog firmware item does.
  • Base Time: One full day (8 hours) of focused work per 1,000 CR of the item's Construction Markup, minimum one day. Gadgeteer halves this. Quick Gadgeteer reduces it to one hour per 1,000 CR, minimum one hour.
  • Modifiers: -1 per component substituted relative to the nearest catalog entry; -2 for a material pairing the tables never use; -1 per function the item's class does not normally carry. Workspace tiers apply as above.
  • Failure: The schematic is scrapped and must be redrawn -- half the base time again, then a new roll.
  • Critical Failure: A hidden flaw. The design reads as sound and builds cleanly, but every item built from it suffers a ghost glitch: it jams, shorts, or overloads on an attack or use roll of 17 or 18 -- a roll that always fails whatever the wielder's skill (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.QD9SOsp2PLsi7llq]{Chapter 1}), so the glitch shows itself only on the worst rolls. The flaw is invisible until it costs someone something in play. Correcting it takes a fresh Design Phase roll at +2, and that correction reaches the schematic only. Items already built keep the flaw, because a corrected drawing does not reach a finished object; a flawed item is put right by Deconstructing it and rebuilding from the corrected Blueprint. A crafter who never notices carries the fault into every unit they make.
  • Proving: An original design is unproven until its first successful build, taking -1 until then. Once proven, that penalty is gone and it builds at the baseline like any proven plan.
  • Output: The schematic is written to a blank Datacard with the write roll of Reading and Writing, above -- a second roll, separate from the design roll that produced it. A failed write costs the hour, not the design: the schematic is still in hand and the write can be re-attempted. The finished Blueprint is Generation 0.

Designing Components: A new component in an existing slot -- a lighter emitter, a cheaper receiver -- is a deeper act of authorship, because everything else builds from the component layer. It follows the Design Phase with three added requirements: the designer must hold Gadgeteer or Quick Gadgeteer; must previously have performed a successful Deconstruction of a component of that class; and the design's cost and capability must still derive -- material weight at @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}'s rate, plus 20 CR per CP for anything granting a trait. Time runs at twice the Design Phase rate, and the design stays unproven until an item built with it has succeeded in real use, not merely been assembled. Better always costs more by construction: a component cannot undercut an existing part except by cheaper material, with the stat consequences the material table dictates.

Copying and Generations: Copying is permitted, and is simply a fresh write: a blank card, the hardware, and a Computer Operation roll at -1 per generation of the source. Data-Crystal is an analog lattice, and every transcription drifts the tolerances it encodes -- each copy is one generation past its source, applied to the build modifier above (0 at Generation 0, -1 at 1, -2 at 2, and so on). At Generation 4 the lattice no longer holds a coherent schematic, and the copy roll fails automatically.

Encoded Blueprints: Commercially sold Blueprints are licensed and lattice-encoded. Copying one first requires a Slicing roll at -4; Failure bricks the blank card, and a Critical Failure also flags the attempt to whoever holds the license. A designer may encode a Blueprint of their own with an hour's work and a Computer Operation roll.

Buying a Blueprint: Every item in this book’s tables has a Blueprint on the market, sold by the same sort of vendor who sells the item -- an armory for weapon schematics, a droid works for chassis and processors, a medical supplier for implants. Availability and legality track the item itself: a restricted weapon’s Blueprint is restricted, a contraband item’s Blueprint is contraband, and a vendor who will not sell you the thing will not sell you the plans for it either.

What It Buys: A purchased Blueprint buys the plan itself -- the schematic every build requires, in hand, lawfully and cheaply -- and the time you did not spend taking an item apart to record it. A catalog item can no more be built without its plan than a custom one; the catalog only makes the plan easy to come by.

Non-Catalog Designs: A Blueprint for something outside this book’s tables has no market price at all: it must be commissioned from its designer, taken from someone who holds one, or authored.

Card Included: As with a program, buying is not a write: the price includes the card, so a purchased Blueprint needs no blank of your own -- only recording, authoring and copying do.

Buying and Selling: The markup is the value of the work (above), and a Blueprint sells the design share of it.

Defining the Markup: Throughout this section, an item's markup means its market price less the cost of its components as the tables list them -- not less the cost of raw material. A Blueprint records how to assemble an item from its parts, not how to make the parts; the Power Cell in a Commlink carries its own maker's design, and its own markup, already. So a Commlink at 1,398 CR built from 233 CR of components has a markup of 1,165 CR for this purpose.

Blueprint Pricing: A Blueprint's price is its media plus its design: 174 CR for the Datacard itself, plus a share of the item's markup for what is written on it. A vendor's catalog Blueprint -- Generation 0, licensed, encoded -- costs 174 CR plus 10% of the markup. An original, non-catalog Blueprint customarily trades at 174 CR plus 50% of the markup for a Generation 0 encoded card; each generation removed halves the design share, and an unencoded card halves it again, but the card itself is never free.

So a Commlink schematic runs 291 CR from a vendor and about 757 CR from its designer, while a schematic for something cheap and simple costs barely more than the blank card it is written on -- which is as it should be, since there is little in it to know.

Trait-Priced Items: For an item priced by the trait rule (20 CR per CP), treat the trait term as its markup.

Programming a Datacard

What This Covers: a Blueprint (above) is one kind of content a Datacard can carry. The others are firmware -- the program a belt, shield, face gadget, implant or droid Processor runs -- and ordinary stored data. All three follow the same shape, because they are the same medium: 174 CR buys the card, and what is written on it is priced and rolled for separately. This section covers writing content outside a build; the crafting chapters cover flashing it into a device.

Reading and Writing: as for Blueprints -- at minimum a Datapad or a proper workstation. A bare Datapad counts as a Basic Toolkit (-2) on the Four Tiers; a workstation is a Dedicated Workshop (+0) or better. Without at least a Datapad the operation is simply impossible.

Blank Card Required: And as for Blueprints, every write needs a blank Datacard in hand before the roll. Authoring a new program, transcribing one you already hold, copying a card and slicing an encoded one all end in a write, and none of them can begin without a card to write to -- there is no way to hold a program that is not on a card.

The Write Roll: A failed write leaves the card undamaged and reusable; a critical failure bricks it pending a Computer Programming roll at -2 to unlock. The write itself is one hour's work and a Computer Operation roll wherever an entry below does not state its own, with workspace tier and Extra Time applying as to any other roll.

Authoring New Firmware: writing a program that does not yet exist is a Computer Programming (IQ/Hard) roll, one full day of focused work per 1,000 CR of the program's Programming Fee, minimum one day. Price a new program by the bands under Costing New Function Firmware (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.sM4JaeipflPpOZgw]{Chapter 13}) or against the closest existing program of similar power. Workspace tiers and Extra Time apply as normal.

Failure: the program will not compile; half the base time again, then a new roll.

Critical Failure: a hidden flaw -- it works on the bench and every device flashed with it suffers a ghost glitch on a use roll of 17 or 18 until the flaw is found and the program rewritten at +2.

Output: as with a Blueprint's Design Phase, the finished program is then written to a blank Datacard with the write roll above -- authoring produces the program, the write puts it on a card, and they are two rolls. A failed write costs the hour and not the work. The card is Generation 0.

Transcribing a Known Program: copying firmware you already have onto a fresh card is a write, not authorship: one hour and a Computer Operation roll. Failure: the write doesn't take; the card is undamaged and can be re-attempted after another hour. Critical Failure: the card is bricked pending a Computer Programming roll at -2 to unlock it.

Copying and Generations: the lattice drifts exactly as it does for Blueprints. Each copy is one generation past its source, the Computer Operation roll takes -1 per generation of the source, and at Generation 4 the lattice no longer holds a coherent program and the copy fails automatically. A card's generation carries into the build: apply -1 per generation to the Firmware Flashing roll of any device flashed from it. A Generation 0 card flashes at no penalty.

Encoded Programs: commercially sold firmware is licensed and lattice-encoded, like a catalog Blueprint. Copying one first requires a Slicing roll at -4; Failure bricks the blank card, and a Critical Failure also flags the attempt to whoever holds the license. An author may encode their own program with an hour's work and a Computer Operation roll.

Buying a Program: media plus content, the same as a Blueprint: 174 CR for the card plus the program's Programming Fee. Availability and legality track the device the program is for. Buying the program is not the same as buying the device -- a finished belt's listed price already includes its Programming Fee, because that is what a buyer pays for the finished thing. A crafter building one either buys the program on a card, copies one they already hold, or authors it. Buying is the one origin that is not a write: the 174 CR is the card, so you receive the card with the program already on it and need no blank of your own. Every other route -- authoring, transcribing, copying, slicing an encoded card -- writes to a blank you must already hold.

Ordinary Data: writing, reading or erasing plain data is a Computer Operation roll with a Datapad or better, and needs no roll at all where nothing is at stake. Encrypting a card of your own takes an hour's work and a Computer Operation roll. Breaking someone else's encryption is a Slicing roll at -4, with the same outcomes as an encoded Blueprint: Failure bricks the card, Critical Failure flags the attempt to whoever holds the key.

Programming Terminals: where a crafting chapter names a Cybernetics Terminal (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.o2ZbGiux36xwNCw0]{Chapter 14}) or a Droid Programming Terminal (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.1ZEtj9W2Z8w75PYC]{Chapter 17}), it is naming a workspace tier for that trade, not a separate item to be bought -- the same way a Dedicated Cyber-Clinic and a Dedicated Tech-Bay are both the +0 tier. Each is the Dedicated Workshop (+0) rung of the Four Tiers for programming work in its trade. A character without one is not barred; they work at a lower tier and take its penalty, exactly as with any other workspace. Only the Datapad or workstation of Reading and Writing above is genuinely required, since without a reader there is no way to touch the card at all.
